title: The Bird That Builds with Mud
standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer such questions as who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.4 word meaning · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A barn swallow builds its nest out of mud. It does not carry the mud in its feet. It carries it in its beak, one small ball at a time.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The bird lands at the edge of a puddle. It picks up mud and grass together. The grass holds the mud, the way sticks hold a wall together.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then it flies to a barn or a bridge. It presses the ball onto the wall and waits. The mud dries hard in the sun.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A nest takes about a thousand trips. Two birds work together for a week or more. The nest ends up shaped like a cup.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The same pair may come back the next year. They fix the old nest instead of building a new one. That saves them a thousand trips.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A barn swallow builds its nest out of mud. It carries the mud in its beak. It takes one small ball at a time.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The bird lands by a puddle. It picks up mud and grass. The grass holds the mud together.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then it flies to a barn. It presses the ball onto the wall. The mud dries hard.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A nest takes about a thousand trips. Two birds work for a week. The nest looks like a cup.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The same pair may come back next year. They fix the old nest. That saves a thousand trips.

questions.q: How does a barn swallow carry mud?
questions.a: It carries the mud in its beak, one small ball at a time.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the puddle) and paragraph D (i.e. a thousand trips).
Summarize how a barn swallow builds a nest.
questions.a: It picks up mud and grass at a puddle, carries one ball at a time in its beak, and presses each ball onto a wall until the mud dries hard. A nest takes about a thousand trips.

questions.q:
beak: the hard mouth of a bird.
puddle: a small pool of water on the ground.
Describe the connection between the grass and the mud.
questions.a: The grass holds the mud together, the way sticks hold a wall together.

note: A thousand trips is the number to put on the board. Ask the class to guess first, then read paragraph D.

title: The First Traffic Light
standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer such questions as who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.4 word meaning · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: The first traffic light in America was turned on in 1914. It stood on a corner in Cleveland, Ohio. It had only two colors, red and green.

paras.label: B
paras.text: There was no yellow light yet. A loud buzzer sounded before the color changed. Drivers heard the buzz and knew to slow down.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A police officer sat in a small booth nearby. He pushed a switch by hand to change the light. The light could not change on its own.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Cars were new then, and so were the rules. Before the light, a police officer stood in the street and waved his arms all day.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Yellow was added a few years later. Today most lights change by themselves, and nobody sits in a booth.

questions.a: It had only red and green, a buzzer sounded before the color changed, and a police officer in a booth pushed a switch by hand to change it.

questions.q:
buzzer: a thing that makes a loud sound to warn people.
booth: a very small room for one person.
Describe the connection between having no yellow light and the buzzer.
questions.a: There was no yellow light yet, so a loud buzzer sounded before the color changed and drivers knew to slow down.

note: Who, what, where and when are all in paragraph A. Let students find each one and say which question it answers.

title: How a Seed Drinks
standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer such questions as who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.4 word meaning · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A seed looks dry and hard. Inside it is a tiny plant, waiting. The plant cannot grow until the seed gets water.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Water soaks in through a small hole in the seed coat. The hole is smaller than the point of a pencil.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The seed swells as it drinks. Sometimes the seed coat splits open. That is the first sign that a seed is alive.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The water wakes up the tiny plant. A root pushes down first, before any leaf comes up. The root looks for more water.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A seed can wait a long time for its drink. Some seeds wait one year. A few kinds have waited hundreds of years.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A seed looks dry and hard. Inside is a tiny plant. It waits for water.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Water soaks in through a small hole. The hole is in the seed coat. It is very small.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The seed swells as it drinks. The seed coat may split open. That means the seed is alive.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The water wakes the tiny plant. A root pushes down first. No leaf comes up yet.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A seed can wait a long time. Some seeds wait a year. A few wait much longer.

questions.q: What does a seed need before it can grow?
questions.a: It needs water, because the tiny plant inside cannot grow until the seed gets a drink.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the small hole) and paragraph D (i.e. the root).
Summarize how a seed starts to grow.
questions.a: Water soaks in through a small hole in the seed coat. The seed swells and the coat may split. Then a root pushes down before any leaf comes up.

questions.q:
seed coat: the hard cover around the outside of a seed.
swell: to get bigger.
Describe the connection between the water and the root.
questions.a: The water wakes up the tiny plant, and a root pushes down first to look for more water.

note: Soak beans overnight and bring them in split. Paragraph C stops being a fact and becomes something on the desk.

title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Lamp
standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer such questions as who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.4 word meaning · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: Before electric lights, a lighthouse burned oil. A keeper lived at the lighthouse and took care of the lamp every single night.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The keeper climbed the stairs at sunset. He filled the lamp with oil and lit the wick. Then he waited and watched.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The glass had to stay clean. Smoke from the flame left a gray film. The keeper wiped the glass many times each night.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Around the lamp sat rings of thick glass. The rings bent the light into one strong beam. Ships could see that beam far out at sea.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A keeper slept in the day. If the lamp went out, a ship might not see the rocks. So someone stayed awake all night, every night.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Long ago a lighthouse burned oil. A keeper lived there. He took care of the lamp every night.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The keeper climbed the stairs at sunset. He filled the lamp with oil. He lit the wick.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The glass had to stay clean. Smoke left a gray film. The keeper wiped it many times.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Rings of thick glass sat around the lamp. They bent the light into one beam. Ships saw it far away.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A keeper slept in the day. If the lamp went out, a ship might hit rocks. Someone stayed awake all night.

questions.q: Why did the keeper wipe the glass?
questions.a: Smoke from the flame left a gray film on the glass, so he wiped it many times each night.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the rings of glass) and paragraph E (i.e. staying awake).
Summarize what a lighthouse keeper did each night.
questions.a: He climbed the stairs at sunset, filled the lamp with oil and lit the wick. He wiped smoke off the glass many times and stayed awake all night.

questions.q:
wick: the string in a lamp that holds the flame.
beam: a line of light that shines out in one direction.
Describe the connection between the rings of glass and the ships.
questions.a: The rings bent the light into one strong beam, so ships could see that beam far out at sea.

note: Why questions are the hardest of the six. Paragraphs C and E both answer one, and both answers are a whole sentence away from the question.

title: Why a Cat Has Whiskers
standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer such questions as who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.4 word meaning · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A cat's whiskers are not just hair. Each one grows from a deep spot in the skin. That spot is full of nerves.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Whiskers feel things the cat does not touch. Moving air bends a whisker a little. The cat knows something is near.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Whiskers also measure. A cat's whiskers are about as wide as its body. If the whiskers fit through a gap, the cat fits too.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A cat uses whiskers most in the dark. Eyes need light. Whiskers work with no light at all.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Whiskers fall out and grow back. That is normal. But a cat with cut whiskers bumps into things.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A cat's whiskers are not just hair. Each one grows deep in the skin. That spot is full of nerves.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Whiskers feel things the cat does not touch. Moving air bends a whisker. The cat knows something is near.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Whiskers also measure. They are as wide as the cat's body. If they fit through a gap, the cat fits.

paras.label: D

paras.label: E
paras.text: Whiskers fall out and grow back. That is normal. A cat with cut whiskers bumps into things.

questions.q: How do whiskers help a cat in the dark?
questions.a: Eyes need light, but whiskers work with no light at all, so a cat uses whiskers most in the dark.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. measuring a gap) and paragraph D (i.e. the dark).
Summarize what a cat's whiskers do.
questions.a: Whiskers feel moving air so a cat knows something is near, and they are about as wide as the cat's body so they measure whether a gap is big enough.

questions.q:
nerve: a part of the body that carries feeling to the brain.
gap: a narrow open space between two things.
Describe the connection between the width of a cat's whiskers and the size of a gap.
questions.a: A cat's whiskers are about as wide as its body, so if the whiskers fit through a gap, the cat fits too.

note: Paragraph E answers a question children ask before they are told not to. Say it plainly: whiskers are never cut.

title: The Mail Comes to Town
standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main topic of a multiparagraph text as well as the focus of specific paragraphs within the text.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.6 author's purpose · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A letter travels a long way before it reaches a door. It makes many stops. Each stop has a job.

paras.label: B
paras.text: First it goes in a blue box on a corner. A truck comes once a day and empties the box into a big bag.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Next it goes to a sorting center. A machine reads the address and sends the letter down the right chute. The machine reads many letters each second.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then it rides in a truck or a plane. A letter going across the country flies at night while the town sleeps.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Last a carrier walks the street with a bag. The carrier knows which houses get mail and which do not. Then the letter is home.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A letter travels a long way. It makes many stops. Each stop has a job.

paras.label: B
paras.text: First it goes in a blue box. A truck comes once a day. It empties the box into a bag.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Next it goes to a sorting center. A machine reads the address. It sends the letter the right way.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then it rides in a truck or a plane. A letter can fly at night.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Last a carrier walks the street. The carrier knows which houses get mail. Then the letter is home.

questions.q: What is this whole text about?
questions.a: It is about the stops a letter makes on its way from a blue box to a door.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the sorting machine) and paragraph E (i.e. the carrier).
Summarize the trip a letter takes.
questions.a: A letter goes into a blue box, a truck empties the box, a machine at a sorting center reads the address, a truck or plane carries it, and a carrier walks it to the door.

questions.q:
sorting: putting things into groups so each one goes the right way.
carrier: the person who brings mail to houses.
Describe the connection between the machine and the chute.
questions.a: The machine reads the address and sends the letter down the right chute, so the letter goes the right way.

note: RI.2.2 wants the topic of the whole text and the focus of one paragraph. Ask for both in the same breath: what is this about, and what is paragraph C about?

title: What a Spider Spins
standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main topic of a multiparagraph text as well as the focus of specific paragraphs within the text.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.6 author's purpose · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A spider makes silk inside its own body. The silk comes out of small spouts at the back. The spider pulls it out with its legs.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Not all silk is the same. One kind is sticky. One kind is dry and strong. A spider makes both in the same web.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The dry lines come first. They hold the web up, like the poles of a tent. The spider walks on those lines.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then the spider adds the sticky spiral. Bugs stick to that part. The spider does not, because it steps on the dry lines.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Many spiders eat the old web at night. The silk goes back into the body. A new web gets built before morning.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A spider makes silk inside its body. The silk comes out at the back. The spider pulls it with its legs.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Not all silk is the same. One kind is sticky. One kind is dry and strong.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The dry lines come first. They hold the web up. The spider walks on those lines.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then the spider adds sticky lines. Bugs stick to them. The spider does not stick.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Many spiders eat the old web at night. Then they build a new one.

questions.q: What is the main topic of this text?
questions.a: It is about the silk a spider makes and how it uses two kinds of silk to build a web.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the dry lines) and paragraph D (i.e. the sticky spiral).
Summarize how a spider builds a web.
questions.a: A spider makes silk inside its body and pulls it out with its legs. It lays dry lines first to hold the web up, then adds a sticky spiral that bugs stick to.

questions.q:
silk: the thin strong thread a spider makes.
spiral: a line that curves around and around.
Describe the connection between the dry lines and the spider not sticking.
questions.a: The spider steps on the dry lines, so it does not stick to the sticky spiral that catches bugs.

note: Most students arrive thinking spiders have oily feet. Paragraph D gives the real answer and it is simpler than the myth.

title: Bread from a Field
standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main topic of a multiparagraph text as well as the focus of specific paragraphs within the text.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.6 author's purpose · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: Bread starts in a field, not a store. A farmer plants wheat in the fall. It grows all through the spring.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In late summer the wheat turns gold. A big machine cuts it and shakes the seeds loose. Those seeds are called grain.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The grain goes to a mill. Heavy wheels crush it into a soft powder. The powder is flour.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A baker mixes flour with water, salt, and yeast. The yeast makes tiny bubbles. The dough puffs up and gets soft.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Heat from the oven sets the bread. The bubbles stay as holes. That is why a slice of bread has holes in it.

paras.text: Bread starts in a field. A farmer plants wheat in the fall. It grows in the spring.

paras.label: B

paras.label: C

questions.a: It is about how bread gets made, from wheat in a field to a slice with holes in it.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the mill) and paragraph D (i.e. the yeast).
Summarize how bread is made.
questions.a: A farmer grows wheat and a machine shakes the grain loose. A mill crushes the grain into flour. A baker mixes flour with water, salt and yeast, and the oven sets the dough.

questions.q:
mill: a place where grain is crushed into flour.
yeast: a tiny living thing that makes dough puff up.
Describe the connection between the yeast and the holes in a slice of bread.
questions.a: The yeast makes tiny bubbles in the dough, and heat from the oven sets the bread so the bubbles stay as holes.

note: Hold up a slice while reading paragraph E. The holes stop being a detail and become the evidence.

title: The Moon Changes Shape
standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main topic of a multiparagraph text as well as the focus of specific paragraphs within the text.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.6 author's purpose · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: The moon looks different every night. Some nights it is a thin curve. Some nights it is a full circle.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The moon does not really change. It is always a ball of rock. Only the lit part changes.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The sun lights up one half of the moon. We see part of that lit half. How much we see depends on where the moon is.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The moon takes about a month to go around the Earth. In that month we see every shape, from thin curve to full circle and back.

paras.label: E
paras.text: You can watch it yourself. Draw the moon every night for a month. Your drawings will show the whole pattern.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The moon looks different each night. Some nights it is a thin curve. Some nights it is round.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The moon does not change. It is a ball of rock. Only the lit part changes.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The sun lights one half of the moon. We see part of that half. It depends on where the moon is.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The moon goes around the Earth in about a month. In that month we see every shape.

paras.label: E
paras.text: You can watch it. Draw the moon each night. Your drawings will show the pattern.

questions.q: Does the moon really change shape?
questions.a: No. The moon is always a ball of rock, and only the lit part that we see changes.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the lit half) and paragraph D (i.e. the month).
Summarize why the moon looks different each night.
questions.a: The sun lights one half of the moon, and we see part of that lit half. How much we see depends on where the moon is as it goes around the Earth in about a month.

questions.q:
curve: a line that bends instead of going straight.
pattern: something that happens again and again in the same order.
Describe the connection between where the moon is and the shape we see.
questions.a: How much of the lit half we see depends on where the moon is, so as it goes around the Earth in a month we see every shape.

note: Paragraph E is an assignment, not a sentence. A month of drawings on the wall teaches this better than any diagram.

title: The Playground Gets Built
standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main topic of a multiparagraph text as well as the focus of specific paragraphs within the text.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.6 author's purpose · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A town wanted a new playground. First the children drew what they wanted. They taped the drawings on the library wall.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Next the town counted the cost. Swings, a slide, and soft ground cost money. The town held a bake sale and asked for help.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then grown-ups picked a spot. It had to be flat. It had to be far from the road.

paras.label: D
paras.text: On a Saturday, forty people came to dig. Some mixed cement. Some held the posts straight while the cement went in.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The playground opened in June. The sign by the gate still has one of the drawings on it.

questions.a: It is about the steps a town took to build a new playground.

note: Five paragraphs, five steps. This is the easiest text in the set for naming what one paragraph is about.

title: What Happens Inside a Cocoon
standard_text:
Standard: Describe the connection between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.5 text features · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A caterpillar eats and eats. It grows so fast that its skin gets tight. It sheds that skin and keeps eating.

paras.label: B
paras.text: When it is big enough, it stops. A moth caterpillar spins silk around itself. That silk case is a cocoon.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Inside, the caterpillar breaks down. Most of its body turns to soft goo. A few small patches of cells are saved.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Those saved patches grow into new parts. One patch becomes a wing. One becomes a leg. One becomes an eye.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Weeks later a moth pushes out. Its wings are wet and folded. It pumps them full and waits for them to dry.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A caterpillar eats and eats. Its skin gets tight. It sheds the skin and eats more.

paras.label: B
paras.text: When it is big enough, it stops. It spins silk around itself. That case is a cocoon.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Inside, the caterpillar breaks down. Most of it turns to goo. A few small patches are saved.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Those patches grow into new parts. One becomes a wing. One becomes a leg.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Weeks later a moth pushes out. Its wings are wet. It pumps them full and waits.

questions.q: What happens to the caterpillar's body inside the cocoon?
questions.a: Most of its body breaks down into soft goo, and a few small patches of cells are saved.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. breaking down) and paragraph D (i.e. the new parts).
Summarize the steps from caterpillar to moth.
questions.a: A caterpillar eats and sheds its skin, then spins a silk cocoon. Inside, most of its body turns to goo while a few patches of cells are saved, and those patches grow into wings and legs before a moth pushes out.

questions.q:
cocoon: the silk case a caterpillar spins around itself.
shed: to drop off something the body no longer needs.
Describe the connection between the saved patches and the moth's wings.
questions.a: The few small patches of cells that are saved grow into new parts, and one of those patches becomes a wing.

note: A butterfly makes a chrysalis, not a cocoon. This text says moth on purpose, and the difference is worth one sentence.

title: From Tree to Pencil
standard_text:
Standard: Describe the connection between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.5 text features · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A pencil starts as a tree. Most pencil wood comes from cedar, because cedar is soft and straight.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The wood is cut into thin flat boards. Each board is about as long as a pencil and as wide as six of them.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A machine cuts narrow grooves into the board. The grooves look like little ditches running side by side.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Gray sticks of graphite are laid in the grooves. A second grooved board is glued on top, like a sandwich.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then a cutter slices the sandwich into six pencils. Paint goes on last, and the eraser is crimped on with a metal ring.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A pencil starts as a tree. Most pencil wood is cedar. Cedar is soft and straight.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The wood is cut into thin flat boards. Each board is as long as a pencil.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A machine cuts narrow grooves in the board. They look like little ditches.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Gray sticks of graphite go in the grooves. A second board is glued on top.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A cutter slices it into six pencils. Paint goes on last. The eraser is added with a metal ring.

questions.q: Why is cedar used for pencils?
questions.a: Cedar is used because it is soft and straight.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the grooves) and paragraph E (i.e. slicing and finishing).
Summarize the steps from tree to pencil.
questions.a: Cedar is cut into thin flat boards, a machine cuts grooves in them, graphite sticks are laid in the grooves, a second board is glued on top, and a cutter slices the sandwich into six pencils.

questions.q:
groove: a long narrow cut in a surface.
graphite: the soft gray stuff that makes a pencil mark.
Describe the connection between the grooves and the graphite.
questions.a: The machine cuts narrow grooves into the board so the gray sticks of graphite can be laid inside them.

note: There is no lead in a pencil and never was. Paragraph D names graphite, and students will ask.

title: How a Puddle Disappears

paras.label: A
paras.text: The rain stops and a puddle sits on the sidewalk. An hour later the puddle is smaller. By the afternoon it is gone.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The water did not sink in. Sidewalk is hard. The water went up into the air instead.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Sun warms the top of the puddle. Warm water bits break away and float off. That is called evaporation.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The water is still there. It is just too small to see. It is now part of the air around you.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Later that air rises and cools. The bits come back together into drops. Those drops make a cloud.

paras.label: B

questions.q: Where does the water in a puddle go?
questions.a: It goes up into the air, because sun warms the top of the puddle and warm water bits break away and float off.

questions.q:
evaporation: when water turns into tiny bits that float in the air.
cool: to get colder.
Describe the connection between the puddle and the cloud.
questions.a: Bits of water float off the puddle into the air, and later that air rises and cools so the bits come back together into drops that make a cloud.

note: Paragraph D is the one that matters. The water is not gone, and students who say gone have missed the whole idea.

title: The Steps of a Fire Drill
standard_text:

paras.label: A
paras.text: A fire drill is practice. Nothing is burning. The school practices so that everyone knows what to do if something ever is.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The alarm sounds first. It is loud on purpose. A quiet alarm would not be heard over a busy room.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Everyone stops and stands. Pencils stay on the desk. Coats stay on the hook, because grabbing things slows the line down.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The teacher takes the class list and leads the line out. The last person out closes the door. A closed door slows a real fire.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Outside, the teacher reads every name. That is the step the whole drill is for. The drill is not over until every name is answered.

questions.q:
drill: practicing something so you will know what to do.
alarm: a loud sound that warns people.
Describe the connection between the closed door and a real fire.
questions.a: The last person out closes the door, and a closed door slows a real fire.

note: Read this before the next drill, not after. Every step has a reason attached, which is what RI.2.3 is asking students to see.

title: How a Tooth Falls Out
standard_text:
Standard: Describe the connection between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text.

 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A baby tooth does not fall out by accident. The body takes it apart on purpose, slowly, from underneath.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A grown-up tooth starts growing in the jaw below. It pushes up toward the baby tooth above it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Cells in the gum dissolve the root of the baby tooth. The root gets shorter and shorter. Nobody can see this happening.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Soon almost no root is left. The tooth is held by a thin piece of gum. That is when it wiggles.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The tooth comes out and the new one keeps rising. A person loses twenty baby teeth this way, one at a time.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A baby tooth does not fall out by accident. The body takes it apart from underneath.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A grown-up tooth grows in the jaw below. It pushes up.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Cells in the gum dissolve the root. The root gets shorter. Nobody can see this.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Soon almost no root is left. A thin bit of gum holds the tooth. That is when it wiggles.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The tooth comes out. The new one keeps rising. A person loses twenty baby teeth.

questions.q: Why does a baby tooth wiggle?
questions.a: Cells in the gum dissolve the root until almost no root is left, and the tooth is held by only a thin piece of gum.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the root) and paragraph D (i.e. the wiggle).
Summarize how a baby tooth falls out.
questions.a: A grown-up tooth grows in the jaw and pushes up. Cells in the gum dissolve the root of the baby tooth until almost none is left, so the tooth wiggles and comes out while the new one keeps rising.

questions.q:
root: the part of a tooth that is under the gum.
dissolve: to break something down until it goes away.
Describe the connection between the grown-up tooth and the baby tooth.
questions.a: The grown-up tooth grows in the jaw below and pushes up toward the baby tooth, while cells in the gum dissolve the baby tooth's root.

note: Every second grader has a stake in this one. Paragraph A is the surprise: the falling out is planned, not an accident.

title: Words on a Street Sign

paras.label: A
paras.text: Street signs use few words. There is no room for a sentence. Each word has to do a lot of work.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Yield means let others go first. It does not mean stop. A driver slows down and waits for a gap.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A sign that says One Way means cars go in one direction only. An arrow on the sign shows which way.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Detour means the usual road is closed. The sign sends you a different way and brings you back to the same road later.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Some signs use no words at all. A picture of a child walking means a school is near. A shape can say as much as a word.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Street signs use few words. There is no room for a sentence. Each word works hard.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Yield means let others go first. It does not mean stop. A driver slows and waits.

paras.label: C
paras.text: One Way means cars go one direction only. An arrow shows which way.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Detour means the road is closed. The sign sends you a different way.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Some signs use no words. A picture of a child means a school is near.

questions.q: What does yield mean?
questions.a: Yield means let others go first; it does not mean stop, so a driver slows down and waits for a gap.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. detour) and paragraph E (i.e. signs with no words).
Summarize what these sign words mean.
questions.a: Yield means let others go first, One Way means cars go in one direction only, and Detour means the usual road is closed and you are sent a different way.

questions.q:
yield: to let someone else go first.
detour: a different route around a closed road.
Describe the connection between the small space on a sign and the words chosen.
questions.a: There is no room for a sentence on a street sign, so each word has to do a lot of work and some signs use a picture instead.

note: Walk the block. Students who have read this will start reading signs they have passed for years.

title: What Nocturnal Means
standard_text:

 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: Some animals sleep at night. Some sleep in the day. An animal that is awake at night and asleep in the day is called nocturnal.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Owls are nocturnal. So are bats, raccoons, and most mice. They hunt and eat while the sun is down.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The opposite word is diurnal. A diurnal animal is awake in the day. People are diurnal.

paras.label: D
paras.text: There is a third word. Crepuscular animals are awake at dawn and dusk. Deer and rabbits often are.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The words tell you when to look. If you want to see a bat, go out at night. A noon walk will not work.

paras.label: A

Summarize the three words in this text.
questions.a: Nocturnal animals are awake at night, diurnal animals are awake in the day, and crepuscular animals are awake at dawn and dusk.

questions.q:
diurnal: awake in the day and asleep at night.
dusk: the time just after the sun goes down.
Describe the connection between knowing the word nocturnal and seeing a bat.
questions.a: The words tell you when to look, so to see a bat you go out at night, because a noon walk will not work.

note: Three words, one idea. Sort classroom animal cards into the three groups and the words stick in one lesson.

title: The Words in a Recipe
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 2 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.2.1 key details · RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.5 text features · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A recipe is a set of orders. Every word is a thing to do. Mixing up two words can ruin the food.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Stir means move it around gently. Beat means move it fast and hard. Eggs for a cake are beaten, not stirred.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Chop means cut into pieces. Dice means cut into small even cubes. Diced is smaller than chopped.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Simmer means keep it just below a boil. A simmer has small bubbles at the edge. A boil has big bubbles all over.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Fold means turn the batter over itself slowly. It keeps the air in. Stirring would push the air out.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A recipe is a set of orders. Every word is a thing to do. The right word matters.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Stir means move it gently. Beat means move it fast and hard.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Chop means cut into pieces. Dice means cut into small cubes. Diced is smaller.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Simmer means just below a boil. A simmer has small bubbles. A boil has big ones.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Fold means turn it over slowly. It keeps the air in.

questions.q: What is the difference between stir and beat?
questions.a: Stir means move it around gently and beat means move it fast and hard, so eggs for a cake are beaten, not stirred.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. chop and dice) and paragraph D (i.e. simmer and boil).
Summarize the recipe words in this text.
questions.a: Stir is gentle and beat is fast and hard. Chop makes pieces and dice makes small even cubes. Simmer is just below a boil, and fold turns batter over slowly to keep the air in.

questions.q:
batter: a soft mix of flour and liquid before it is cooked.
cube: a small block with flat square sides.
Describe the connection between folding and the air in a batter.
questions.a: Folding turns the batter over itself slowly so it keeps the air in, while stirring would push the air out.

note: Act the verbs out with an empty bowl. Stir, beat and fold look different from across the room.

title: Words for Baby Animals
standard_text:

paras.label: A
paras.text: Many baby animals have their own name. The name is not the same as the grown-up name. Knowing both helps you read.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A baby cat is a kitten. A baby dog is a puppy. A baby duck is a duckling.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Some names are used for more than one animal. A young goat and a young antelope are both called a kid. A young deer is a fawn.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Other names are a surprise. A baby swan is a cygnet. A baby owl is an owlet. A baby kangaroo is a joey.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A few animals share one word. A baby seal, whale, or elephant is a calf, the same word used for a baby cow.

questions.q:

calf: a baby cow, seal, whale or elephant.

note: Paragraph E is the useful one. One word doing several jobs is the thing that trips readers up later.

paras.label: B

paras.label: C
paras.text: A watch is not a warning. A watch means the weather could happen. A warning means it is happening now.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Wind chill is not the real temperature. It is how cold the air feels when wind is blowing on your skin.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Scattered showers means rain in some places, not everywhere. Your street may stay dry while the next town gets wet.

topic: the thing a part of a book is about.

title: Why Some Words Are Bold

paras.label: D
paras.text: Bold words often show up again in the glossary. The author bolded them so you could find them twice.

paras.text: A glossary is a small dictionary inside a book. It only holds the words that book uses. It sits near the back.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The words are in ABC order. Each word has a short meaning next to it. The meaning fits that book.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That last part matters. The word bed means one thing in a sleep book and another in a river book. A glossary gives the one you need.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A glossary is faster than a dictionary. A dictionary holds thousands of words. A glossary holds the few that are hard in this book.

paras.label: E
paras.text: If a word is bold on the page, check the glossary. The author put it there for you.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the word bed) and paragraph D (i.e. faster than a dictionary).
Summarize what a glossary does.
questions.a: A glossary near the back lists the hard words of that book in ABC order with a short meaning for each, and the meaning fits that book rather than every book.

questions.q:
dictionary: a book that tells what many words mean.
meaning: what a word stands for.
Describe the connection between a bold word and the glossary.
questions.a: If a word is bold on the page, check the glossary, because the author put it there for you.

paras.label: A
paras.text: An icon is a tiny picture that stands for a job. You tap it and something happens. There are no words on most of them.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A magnifying glass means search. A house means go back to the start. A gear means settings.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Icons work in every language. A picture of a trash can means delete whether you read English or not.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Some icons come from old objects. The save icon is a floppy disk, a thing almost nobody has used in thirty years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: If an icon is new to you, hold your finger on it. Many screens will show the word for a second.

title: A Sign That Asks You to Help
standard_text:

paras.label: A
paras.text: A sign at the park says: Please carry out what you carry in. The sign is short. It has one job.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The sign is not there to explain trash. It is not there to describe the park. It is there to ask you to do something.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Under the big words there is a smaller line. It says that a bag left behind can harm the birds that pick at it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That line is the reason. The author gave one reason, not five, because a sign has to be read while walking.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Think about why a thing was written. Signs ask. Maps show. Books often explain. The purpose shapes every word.

title: How to Wash Your Hands
standard_text:

paras.label: A
paras.text: This text has one purpose. It is not here to tell a story and not here to describe a place. It is here to explain how to do something.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Wet your hands first. Then add soap. Soap is the part that does the work.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Rub for twenty seconds. That is about as long as singing the ABC song once. Most people stop too soon.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Soap does not kill most germs. It makes them slide off, because soap lets water grab on to grease and dirt.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Rinse and dry. Drying matters, because wet hands pick up more germs from what they touch next.

note: Paragraph D corrects what most students believe. Soap is not a poison, it is a handle.

title: A Letter to the Principal

paras.label: A
paras.text: A second grade class wrote a letter to their principal. They wanted a water fountain put in near the field.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The letter did not tell a story and did not describe the school. It asked for one thing and gave two reasons for it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The first reason was distance. The nearest fountain is inside the building, all the way down two halls.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second reason was time. Recess is twenty minutes, and walking in and out uses five of them.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The class wrote one more line at the end. They offered to help pick the spot. That offer was a reason too.

title: What a Field Guide Is For
standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main purpose of a text, including what the author wants to answer, explain, or describe.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.5 text features · RI.2.8 reasons · RI.2.10 comprehension

paras.label: A
paras.text: A field guide is a book for naming things. It does not tell you a story about a bird. It helps you say which bird it was.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The pages are built for speed. Pictures sit on one side. Short notes sit on the other.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each note lists the things that are easy to see. Size. Color. The shape of the beak. Where it lives.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A field guide leaves most things out on purpose. It does not say what the bird dreams or how it feels.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The purpose decides what goes in. A book made to help you name a bird looks nothing like a book made to tell its story.

field guide: a book that helps you name plants or animals you see.
beak: the hard mouth of a bird.
Describe the connection between the purpose of a book and what goes inside it.

note: Put a field guide and a story about a bird side by side. Paragraph E becomes obvious in ten seconds.

title: The Museum Map
standard_text:

paras.label: A
paras.text: At the door of a museum, someone hands you a map. The map is one page. It was made with one purpose.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The map does not describe the art. It does not explain who painted it. It shows you where things are.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Rooms are drawn as boxes with numbers. A small key tells you what each number holds.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Icons mark the things you will need. A fork means food. A letter W means water. An arrow means the way out.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The signs inside the rooms do the other job. Those explain the art. The map gets you to the room, and the sign takes over.

note: Two texts, two purposes, one building. That pairing is what makes paragraph E worth reading twice.

title: The Picture That Shows the Inside
standard_text:
Standard: Explain how specific images, such as a diagram showing how a machine works, contribute to and clarify a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.5 text features · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: Some pictures in a science book look like something has been sliced open. A seed, a volcano, or a tooth is shown cut in half.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That kind of picture is called a cutaway. Nothing was really cut. The artist drew away one side so you can see in.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A cutaway does a job words cannot. A sentence can say a seed has a tiny plant inside. The picture shows you where.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Small labels point to the parts. A line runs from each word to the exact spot it names.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Read the picture and the words together. If the words say root and the label says root, you have found the same thing twice.

cutaway: a drawing that shows the inside of a thing.
label: a word on a picture that names one part.
Describe the connection between the words on the page and the labels on the picture.
questions.a: If the words say root and the label says root, you have found the same thing twice, so reading them together tells you where the part is.

note: Cut an apple in half and set it beside a cutaway drawing. Paragraph B stops being a trick and becomes obvious.

title: The Map Next to the Story
standard_text:
Standard: Explain how specific images, such as a diagram showing how a machine works, contribute to and clarify a text.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A book about a long journey often has a map beside the words. The map is not there to look nice.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The words can say the family travelled for six weeks. The map shows how far six weeks took them.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A dotted line usually marks the route. Dots or stars mark the places where they stopped.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A map also shows what is not in the words. You can see a mountain range the family had to cross even if no sentence says so.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Look at the map before you read, and again at the end. The second look is the one that makes the story fit together.

title: Arrows in a Diagram
standard_text:

paras.label: A
paras.text: An arrow in a diagram is not decoration. It means something exact. It usually means this goes here next.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In a water cycle diagram, arrows carry water from the sea to a cloud to the ground and back.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Arrows can also mean push. In a picture of a machine, an arrow may show which way a part is being pressed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The size of an arrow can matter too. A thick arrow may mean a lot. A thin one may mean a little.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Follow the arrows in order before reading the words. The order they make is the thing the diagram is about.

title: Then and Now Pictures
standard_text:

paras.label: A
paras.text: Some history books put two pictures side by side. One of them is old. The other was taken from the same spot today.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The pair does something one picture cannot. It shows change without saying a word about it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Look for what stayed. A church, a hill, or a bend in the river is often in both pictures.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then look for what went. A streetcar line, a row of trees, or a whole block of houses may be gone.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The things that stayed are how you know it is the same place. The things that went are the story.

note: A local pair works best. Photograph the view outside the school and set it beside an old picture of the same corner.

title: A Picture That Shows Size

paras.label: A
paras.text: A picture of an animal does not tell you how big it is. A beetle and a bear can fill the same page.

paras.label: B
paras.text: So books add something for scale. A small drawing of a hand, a coin, or a person stands next to the animal.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Now the page means something. If the beetle is half as long as a hand, you know.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Some books use a ruler line instead. A short bar under the picture is marked with inches or centimeters.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Always look for the scale before you decide a thing is huge. Without it, every picture is the size of the page.

questions.a: Some of its roots block most of the salt and some of its leaves push salt out, which dries in white crystals. Because the mud holds almost no air, it also grows roots that stick up out of the water to breathe.

questions.q:
mangrove: a tree that grows in salt water near a coast.
crystal: a small hard piece that forms as something dries.
Describe the connection between the tangled roots and a storm wave.
questions.a: The tangled roots slow a storm wave before it reaches land, and young fish hide between them.

note: Two problems, two solutions, and then a paragraph about everyone else. That shape is worth naming out loud.

paras.text: There is an island in Michigan where cars have been against the law since 1898. About five hundred people live there all year.

paras.text: People get around on bicycles, on foot, and in carriages pulled by horses. There are more than five hundred horses on the island in summer.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Everything arrives by boat. Furniture, food, and building supplies are unloaded at a dock and moved by wagon.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Even an emergency runs on horses. The ambulance is a sled in winter and a horse-drawn wagon the rest of the year.

paras.text: The rule started because the first cars frightened the horses. It stayed because people decided they liked the island the way it was.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Some ants do not hunt for food. They grow it. Leafcutter ants have been farming for millions of years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A line of ants carries pieces of leaf back to the nest. The leaves are not what they eat. They cannot digest a leaf at all.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Underground, the ants chew the leaves into a soft mush. They plant a fungus in it. The fungus grows, and that is the food.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The nest is kept clean on purpose. Workers pull out any mold that is not the right kind and carry it far away.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A big nest can hold millions of ants and reach deeper than a person is tall. All of it is built around one crop.

Describe the connection between the leaves and the ants' food.
questions.a: The ants cannot digest a leaf, so they chew the leaves into mush and plant a fungus in it, and the fungus is what they eat.

note: Paragraph B is the twist. Every student will assume the ants eat the leaves, and the second sentence says no.

paras.label: A
paras.text: For a long time, libraries had no room for children. Many would not let anyone under fourteen through the door at all.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In 1890, a librarian in Brookline, Massachusetts set aside one room with low shelves and small chairs. It was one of the first.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The idea spread quickly. Within thirty years most city libraries had a children's room, and some had a librarian who worked only there.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Those librarians changed what got published. They asked for books with bigger print and better pictures, and companies made them.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A children's room looks ordinary now. It was an argument once, and somebody had to win it.
